content.text: React doesn't store state inside your component function. It stores it at a position in the UI tree and keeps it for as long as the same component type renders there, however its props change. To get fresh state for a different item, give the component a key; to keep state after a component disappears, store it higher up.

A support agent opens Alice's ticket and starts a reply: "Hi Alice, your refund was approved…". A chat pings, she clicks Bob's ticket in the sidebar, and the screen switches to Bob: his name, his order, his message history. Everything except the reply box, which still holds the text written for Alice. She skims it, hits Send, and Bob gets someone else's refund news. The component is
, and the developer who wrote it was sure that a different ticket meant a different reply box.
The belief: state lives inside the component, the way fields live inside an object. Render
and you have a new component with new state. Whether state is kept or reset depends on what you render.
It's a natural model. Class components really did keep
on an instance, and a JSX tag looks a lot like a constructor call.
sits inside the function body, so it reads like a local variable the function owns. And part of it is true: state is isolated per component, so two
tags side by side each count on their own. The mistake is in what React treats as "one component": not the props, not the data on screen, and not the line of JSX you wrote.
React holds the state, not your function
From your JSX, React builds a
: which component sits under which. Your component function is called on every render and keeps nothing between calls. When it calls

, React hands it the value stored for that spot in the tree. React's docs state the rule plainly: a component keeps its state for as long as it's rendered at its position in the UI tree. Remove it, or render a different component type at that position, and React discards the state.
Same type, same position: the state stays
On every render, React compares the new tree with the previous one position by position, as part of
. If the same component type sits at the same position, React treats it as the same component: it passes the new props and keeps the state. That's the support bug.

doesn't help either: React uses it on the first render and ignores it afterwards.
Position is in the tree, not in your JSX
Two lines of JSX can be one position. If an
from one branch and the same structure from the other, both land as the same child of the same parent, so the state carries over. A ternary works the same way:
is one slot with one state.

moves the component to the other slot, so it starts over. And as the first article in this path showed, changing the element type above a component, like a
A key turns "same position" into "same item"

isn't only for lists. On any component, it adds an identity on top of the position: React keeps the state only when both the type and the key match. A reply to Alice is conceptually a different reply box from one to Bob, so say so:

Keeping state after a component disappears

Sometimes you want the opposite: drafts that survive switching tickets, one per ticket. State dies with its position, so it has to live in something that stays mounted. The usual answer is to store it one level up and key the data, not the component:

This time the same-position rule works for you: the panel's state survives every switch, and each ticket reads its own entry. React's docs list two more options: hide inactive views with CSS instead of unmounting them, or keep drafts in
so they survive a reload too.
and cleans up their Effects, but keeps their state, so a tab or panel comes back exactly as the user left it.
How to apply it in your project

items.title: Look for state that leaks between items

content.text: Switch between two records on every master-detail screen: tickets, contacts, products. Typed text, a selected tab, an open section or a scroll position that follows you to the next record is state staying at its position.

items.title: Key the view where the item changes

content.text: on the component that represents one item, as high in the tree as the reset should reach. Everything below it starts fresh for each item.
Search for Effects whose only job is calling setters when a prop changes, like
. A key on the component usually removes them entirely.

items.title: Decide which state must outlive its component

content.text: If users expect a draft or a filter to survive switching away, store it per id in a parent that stays mounted, or hide the view instead of unmounting it.
